newsitem.title: FRANCE: France hopeful talks can restore peace to Congo.
newsitem.headline: France hopeful talks can restore peace to Congo.

text.p: France said on Monday it was hopeful that a diplomatic initiative in Gabon could restore peace and safeguard democracy in the Congolese capital of Brazzaville as it began pulling its troops out of the country.

"As we have constantly said, we fully support the mediation effort undertaken by (Gabonese) President (Omar) Bongo in conjunction with Mr Mohamed Sahnoun, special representative of the United Nations," the French Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
"An immediate return to democracy via a presidential election is essential to the future of Congo," it said.
The ministry said Paris was prepared to help organise and carry out the presidential election scheduled for July 27 in its former colony. It also was prepared to provide emergency humanitarian aid.
Several African leaders were joining representatives of the warring Congolese factions on Monday for peace talks in the Gabon capital Libreville hosted by Bongo.
The meeting was likely to consider a call from Congo President Pascal Lissouba for deployment of an African peace force, officials in Librevillle said.
France has rejected a request from Lissouba to leave its troops to act as a buffer force in Brazzaville and has said all its 1,200 troops would pull out of Congo.

A French Defence Ministry spokesman said the troops had begun withdrawing from Brazzaville on Monday morning. Among the first to leave were 306 marines who were being flown to the Chad capital Ndjamena and then on to France, the spokesman said.

French troops had been standing by for weeks in Brazzaville for a possible evacuation of foreigners from the neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo as President Laurent Kabila's rebels took power Kinshasa.

In the event, the violence broke out in Brazzaville on June 5, and Paris quickly built up its forces to protect its nationals from the fighting between Congolese soldiers and supporters of former Marxist military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso.

The French troops' mission soon turned into one of helping to evacuate thousands of foreign residents from the central African nation as bloody fighting continued despite international mediation efforts.
The Foreign Ministry said French forces had helped evacuate 5,666 people from Brazzaville in a mission dubbed Pelican II.

"All those who wanted to leave have left," ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt said. "There were no casualties. The operation was a successs." One French soldier was killed and five were wounded in the fighting.
Those evacuated included 1,523 French nationals, 174 Lebanese, 162 Russians, 94 Belgians and 65 Americans.
The Defence Ministry said the French troops and non-combat equipment were being flown out in two C-130 Hercules transport aircraft, each of which was to make 16 round-trips on Monday.
Communications and logistics units were also scheduled to leave on Monday, headed for Libreville, the ministry said.
